articles.title: Watch: E-bike battery explodes into massive fireball inside Oregon home
articles.summary: Surveillance footage from inside the home shows a mother and son noticing smoke coming from the battery before it suddenly bursts into flames.
articles.body:
Home surveillance footage shows the moment an e-bike battery burst into flames and exploded inside a home in Troutdale, Oregon. After investigating a strange smell, a mother and son notice smoke coming from the battery before it erupts into a huge fireball, followed by smaller explosions.

A second angle shows the battery charging moments before the blast, as occupants rush to escape. All six people in the home got out safely, though a cat died in the fire, according to local reports.

articles.title: Delegados da PF: ADPF critica afastamento após relatórios do STF | G1
articles.standfirst: ADPF afirma que explicações da corporação são insuficientes e critica decisão de refazer relatórios sobre ministros do STF citados no caso Master. PF diz que afastamentos são atos de gestão e que troca nas chefias não altera equipes dos inquéritos.
articles.summary: A ADPF afirma que a troca de comando na repressão à corrupção, ocorrida após menções a ministros do STF no caso Master, fere a autonomia dos delegados da PF.
articles.body:
A Associação Nacional dos Delegados de Polícia Federal (ADPF) criticou o afastamento de dois delegados de funções de chefia na área de combate à corrupção da Polícia Federal e afirmou que o episódio pode representar uma ameaça à autonomia dos responsáveis pelas investigações.

Em nota, a entidade questiona as circunstâncias dos afastamentos e a decisão de refazer relatórios produzidos pela PF sobre menções a ministros do Supremo Tribunal encontradas nas investigações do caso Master.

Segundo interlocutores da corporação, a PF vai refazer os relatórios, que serão individualizados sobre todos os ministros do STF que tenham sido citados , e não apenas Alexandre de Moraes, Kassio Nunes Marques e Dias Toffoli.

🔎A ADPF é uma associação criada para representar e defender as prerrogativas, a autonomia e os interesses dos delegados da PF. A associação também atua no debate sobre projetos de lei e em causas na Justiça ligadas à categoria.

"A ADPF considera o episódio especialmente grave pelo precedente que pode representar. A possibilidade de retaliação a delegados em razão das pessoas mencionadas nas investigações transmite uma mensagem preocupante à carreira e ameaça um dos pilares fundamentais da Polícia Federal: a autonomia de suas autoridades policiais para investigar, independentemente de quem sejam os envolvidos", diz em nota.

Os delegados Daniel Cola e Wedson Cajé foram afastados de funções na Coordenação-Geral de Repressão à Corrupção, Crimes Financeiros e Lavagem de Dinheiro no dia seguinte à conclusão dos relatórios. A PF nega que o material esteja pronto.

Segundo fontes, eles elaboraram os relatórios.

Os relatórios reuniam citações aos ministros Dias Toffoli, Alexandre de Moraes e Kassio Nunes Marques e apresentavam fatos com indícios de crime, sem atribuir responsabilidade aos ministros.

A ADPF afirma que as justificativas apresentadas pela Polícia Federal até agora são "insuficientes" para explicar tanto os afastamentos quanto a decisão de refazer os documentos.

A entidade afirma que não contesta a prerrogativa da direção da PF de substituir ocupantes de funções de chefia, mas que mudanças não podem ocorrer em razão de divergências jurídicas entre os responsáveis pelas investigações e a direção do órgão.

Segundo a associação, cabe aos delegados responsáveis pelos procedimentos definir a condução das investigações, dentro das atribuições legais de cada autoridade.

A ADPF também afirma que não caberia ao diretor-geral da PF interferir no conteúdo ou determinar a reformulação de documentos elaborados no exercício da atividade de polícia judiciária.

"O episódio também evidencia, na avaliação da entidade, uma postura recorrente da atual direção da Polícia Federal, marcada por atos que contrariam princípios historicamente observados pela instituição, como o respeito à condução dos inquéritos por seus respectivos presidentes e o necessário distanciamento da gestão em relação à atividade de polícia judiciária", afirma a associação.

A PF vai refazer os relatórios com referências a integrantes do Supremo. Segundo interlocutores da corporação, a avaliação da Polícia Federal é que os documentos anteriores não seguiram os critérios definidos pelo presidente do STF , ministro Edson Fachin .

Os relatórios serão individualizados sobre todos os ministros do STF que tenham sido citados, e não apenas Alexandre de Moraes, Kassio Nunes Marques e Dias Toffoli. O blog do Valdo Cruz mostrou que também há menções aos ministros André Mendonça, Luiz Fux e Gilmar Mendes .

Os novos relatórios vão apresentar as referências aos ministros em trocas de mensagens com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro e os contextos em que elas aparecem, com informações como a identidade do interlocutor, a data e o horário da conversa.

➡️ Para respeitar os critérios definidos por Fachin, os relatórios não vão trazer nenhum tipo de análise sobre o conteúdo dessas mensagens.

Em nota publicada nesta segunda-feira (9), a PF afirmou que não comenta atos de gestão de pessoal e disse que dispensas de funções de confiança são baseadas em critérios de "conveniência e oportunidade administrativa".

A corporação também afirmou que as mudanças nas chefias não alteram as equipes responsáveis pelos inquéritos em andamento, inclusive aqueles relacionados às operações Compliance Zero e Sem Desconto.

Sede da Polícia Federal, em Brasília — Foto: Marcos Oliveira/Agência Senado

articles.title: TSE multa Meta: Relator vota por punição de R$ 7,5 milhões | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa teria deixado de cumprir prazos fixados pelo TSE para adotar medidas que garantissem tratamento igualitário entre os presidenciáveis na disputa eleitoral. Decisão foi tomada por unanimidade.
articles.summary: TSE multa Meta em R$ 7,5 milhões após voto de relator por falhas no tratamento isonômico das campanhas de Lula e Bolsonaro no segundo turno das eleições 2022.
articles.body:
O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) decidiu nesta terça-feira (10), por unanimidade, multar em R$ 7,5 milhões a empresa Meta (dona do Facebook, WhatsApp e Instagram) por descumprimento de decisões da Corte durante as eleições.

Os ministros seguiram o voto do relator, ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze, para aplicar a punição à empresa Meta por deixar de cumprir integralmente determinações da Corte para garantir isonomia na disputal presidencial, substituindo prazos judiciais fixados pelo TSE por prazos próprios, além de falta de transparência.

Além disso, afirma que a empresa apresentou informações de forma fracionada ao tribunal, em linguagem estrangeira e técnica, o que dificultou a verificação de dificuldades técnicas apontadas para justificar falhas.

Os ministros analisaram uma ação da campanha do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que foi reeleito, e aponta que houve um tratamento desigual na distribuição de conteúdos políticos e na veiculação de anúncios eleitorais durante o segundo turno das eleições .

Segundo Bellizze, "as plataformas digitais exercem poder informacional que condiciona, por sistemas algorítmicos pouco transparentes, a circulação da informação política e a formação da vontade do eleitor".

"A proteção do pluralismo político, da igualdade de oportunidades entre candidaturas e da autonomia do eleitor exige mecanismos efetivos de governança algorítmica, de auditoria e de fiscalização que permitam verificar o cumprimento dos deveres de transparência e de cuidado", disse.

O ministro afirmou que as regras do TSE impõem aos provedores deveres voltados à proteção da integridade do processo eleitoral , que decorrem de sua função social e de seu dever de cuidado. Com isso, considera que a imposição de multa e de outras medidas necessárias é indispensável para assegurar o cumprimento das decisões desta Justiça especializada.

Para o ministro, o caso da Meta "revelou a dificuldade de tornar efetivas as providências impostas, cumpridas, em grande parte, após os prazos, de forma incompleta ou mediante declarações cuja verificação depende de dados que somente a representada detém".

Bellizze afirmou ainda que nesta ação não é possível apontar que a Meta atuou de forma deliberada para desequilibrar o pleito , que isso depende de produção de prova robusta, o que não é possível no processo que está em análise.

Vice-presidente do TSE, o ministro André Mendonça afirmou que, durante as eleições, sentiu resistência da Meta em cumprir as determinações da Corte.

"A importância do cumprimento das decisões judiciais é o eixo central. Eu confesso que durante as eleições eu tive a percepção de que não era tao simples o cumprimento das decisões, não pelo conteúdo em si, mas uma certa resistência por parte da empresa".

A campanha petista acusou a plataforma de restringir seletivamente a distribuição de publicações ligadas ao seu campo político e de descumprir obrigações previstas na legislação eleitoral. Além disso, questiona limitações no impulsionamento de anúncios de campanha e possíveis diferenças no tratamento dado às candidaturas.

A advogada Patrícia Martins afirmou que todas as ordens da Corte foram devidamente cumpridas pela empresa, que no processo não foi apontado nenhum direcionamento político e que ocorreram apenas falhas técnicas corrigidas de forma breve e devidamente explicadas .

"São falsas alegações de que a Meta interferiu ou favoreceu em nome de qualquer candidato ou grupo político. A Meta continuará cumprindo a legislação brasileira, corrigindo erros quando existirem e garantindo igualitária de todos os espectros políticos", disse.

O advogado da campanha do presidente, Angelo Ferraro, disse que o julgamento não trata de anúncios, mas envolve a soberania nacional e a liberdade do voto.

"Nessa eleição a Meta deixou de ser plataforma e passou a ser agente político e aparentemente escolheu um lado. O Brasil não é colônia de ninguém e seu presidente não será escolhido pelo Vale do Silício ou Washington. Nenhuma nação soberana admite isso, muito menos que uma empresa internacional influencie o voto", afirmou.

Durante a campanha eleitoral, Bellizze chegou a determinar que a Meta garantisse tratamento igualitário entre as campanhas de Lula e do candidato derrotado Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) . A decisão foi mantida por unanimidade pelo TSE.

Mesmo depois da determinação do tribunal, a Procuradoria-Geral Eleitoral (PGE) avaliou que a empresa Meta deixou de cumprir parte das determinações da Corte para o tratamento de conteúdo das campanhas presidenciais no segundo turno e que havia indicativo de nova violação de isonomia no uso da ferramenta de inteligência artificial.

Na avaliação do MPE, a empresa descumpriu determinações “por reconhecimento expresso ou implícito da própria representada”.

Segundo a Procuradoria, não foram adotados:

processamento isonômico das denúncias e relatório dos canais;

informe individualizado dos anúncios reavaliados e suspensos;

informe das providências concretamente adotadas;

reapresentação do relatório sigiloso em língua portuguesa.

Justiça de São Paulo proíbe Meta de usar conteúdo jornalístico sem autorização — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

articles.title: Relator atende agronegócio, e MP que renegocia dívidas rurais é aprovada na Câmara | G1
articles.standfirst: Líder do governo incluiu alterações pedidas por parlamentares ligados ao setor; deputados também incluíram trecho sobre exportação de insumos para vapes.
articles.summary: Líder do governo incluiu alterações pedidas por parlamentares ligados ao setor; deputados também incluíram trecho sobre exportação de insumos para vapes.
articles.body:
Depois de uma longa negociação, a Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira (10) a Medida Provisória (MP) que renegocia as dívidas rurais . O líder do Governo na Câmara, Paulo Pimenta (PT-RS), aceitou pedidos do setor do agronegócio e apresentou um texto de meio-termo.

Integrantes da Frente Parlamentar do Agronegócio (FPA) mantiveram críticas ao texto aprovado. Ainda assim, a maioria de seus membros aprovou o texto, já que a MP deixa de valer na quarta-feira (11) caso não seja aprovada até o fim do prazo . Agora, a medida ainda segue para análise pelo plenário do Senado.

Entre as mudanças feitas pelo texto aprovado está a prorrogação do prazo para a contratação da linha de crédito para o pagamento das dívidas . Antes, limitado a 120 dias a partir da criação da lei, o prazo agora será prorrogável por mais 120 dias.

Esse era um pedido da FPA, que indicava que, do total de R$ 100 bilhões destinados à renegociação, pouco mais de 20% – ou seja, R$ 20 bilhões – foram contratados desde que a MP entrou em vigor. A ideia, segundo deputados e senadores, é dar mais tempo e condições para que os produtores rurais façam a adesão ao programa de renegociação de dívidas.

"Essa Medida Provisória não é a que gostaríamos", disse a senadora Tereza Cristina (PP-MS) durante a análise do relatório na comissão mista sobre o tema mais cedo nesta terça-feira. "Hoje estamos aprovando um texto que vai resolver uma parte, vai atender uma parte dos endividados".

Outro pedido da frente agropecuária atendido foi a flexibilização de laudos para comprovar a perda de duas ou mais safras ou de 30% da renda por eventos climáticos ou pela alteração dos preços . Agora, laudos coletivos serão aceitos para a renegociação de dívidas de micro, mini, pequeno e médio produtor rural.

Segundo Pimenta, as mudanças feitas no relatório não acarretam aumento dos custos para o orçamento público. O líder do Governo destacou o diálogo com o Ministério da Fazenda para a construção do texto e indicou que a ideia é manter o custo de R$ 100 bilhões definido inicialmente pelo governo.

"Evidentemente, não é um texto que agrada a todos e a todas, mas que, do meu ponto de vista, é um texto que avançou muito no sentido de que a gente possa alcançar o objetivo principal da medida provisória, que é fazer essa renegociação", disse Pimenta.

Texto foi aprovado por comissão especial nesta terça-feira e, no mesmo dia, pelo plenário da Câmara. — Foto: Renato Araújo/Câmara dos Deputados

Em pontos que parlamentares ligados ao agroneócios queriam mudanças, como os juros e os limites para dívidas de acordo com a categoria de produtores, Pimenta não recuou. O líder do governo também não incluiu um fundo garantidor contra possíveis perdas futuras do agro.

A FPA indicou que continuará tentando, a partir de outros projetos, alterar pontos que considera importantes para os produtores rurais brasileiros.

Entre as mudanças incluídas por Paulo Pimenta está uma alteração na lei que cria a Anvisa (Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária) para permitir a produção nacional de insumos utilizados para a produção de cigarros eletrônicos e vapes, que são proibidos no Brasil.

Como inicialmente a MP tratava somente das dívidas de produtores rurais, a inclusão da liberação de produção de insumos para vapes pode ser vista como um "jabuti", ou seja, um tema que não fazia parte do texto inicial. Assim, questionamentos na Justiça sobre esse trecho da lei são possíveis.

A alteração na lei libera a produção desses insumos utilizando tabaco somente para a exportação. Pimenta afirmou ao g1 que a mudança não abre espaço para a produção e uso de vapes no Brasil. Segundo ele, a inclusão do tema na MP foi um pedido de produtores do país e é somente para a exportação dos materiais, com a Anvisa mantendo o poder para definir a comercialização em território nacional.

O relator do projeto na comissão especial, o deputado e líder do governo na Câmara Paulo Pimenta (PT-RS) — Foto: Renato Araújo/Câmara dos Deputados

A aprovação na comissão mista no início da tarde desta quarta-feira (10) foi acompanhada de tensão entre integrantes da FPA. O deputado Afonso Hamm (PP-RS) criticou o acordo com o governo. Para ele, o texto acordado tinha avanços "muito tímidos" e declarou voto contra – o único da comissão.

"Nós fizemos, eu fiz várias emendas, e vários fizeram – e elas todas foram rejeitadas. Tem algum aproveitamento, mas é muito pouco", disse o deputado. "É impossível votar a favor".

Pedro Lupion (Republicanos-PR), presidente da FPA, criticou a fala do colega: "Se todos nós votarmos contra, não passa a medida provisória. Você fica fazendo média e a gente fica de idiota."

A FPA já tinha indicado que deixar a MP caducar e o programa de renegociação perder a validade seria visto como responsabilidade da frente , já que o governo considera que fez sua parte ao fazer o programa de renegociação das dívidas.

articles.title: Escala 6x1: Dino sinaliza que decisão em ação que questiona transição da nova jornada de trabalho sai até sexta | G1
articles.standfirst: Relator das ações que pedem o adiamento do início da implementação da nova escala conduziu audiência de conciliação com representantes de empregadores e de trabalhadores.
articles.summary: Relator das ações que pedem o adiamento do início da implementação da nova escala conduziu audiência de conciliação com representantes de empregadores e de trabalhadores.
articles.body:
Ministro Flávio Dino, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), em sessão plenária do 21 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Gustavo Moreno/STF

O ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Flávio Dino, afirmou nesta terça-feira (10) que publicará até sexta-feira (13) uma decisão na ação que discute o período de transição para a implementar a escala 5x2.

Dino é relator dos pedidos feitos por entidades do setor produtivo para que seja concedido mais prazo para a adapatação à nova jornada de trabalho.

Paras regras, os empregadores têm 60 dias a partir da promulgação, ou seja, até 16 de dezembro, para reduzir a jornada de 44 para 42 horas semanais. A diminuição para 40 horas semanais passará a valer em dezembro de 2027.

Dino quer levar o assunto ao plenário do STF

O ministro disse também que vai pedir na próxima semana para o presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, pautar o mérito da ação no plenário. Cabe ao presidente da Corte decidir a data do julgamento.

“Por conta desse cronograma exíguo e talvez até para facilitar a atividade do Poder Executivo na edição do decreto, nós vamos publicar até sexta-feira e vou imediatamente submeter a referendo do plenário. Ficará a critério do presidente, se chama o chamado PV [plenário virtual] ou se faz tudo numa sentada só no plenário presencial, não está na minha zona de governança”, declarou Dino.

Dino conduziu uma audiência de conciliação nesta terça no STF com confederações de diversos setores e centrais sindicais de trabalhadores.

Segundo antecipou o ministro, a decisão deve abordar principalmente dois temas:

a garantia mínima de que não haverá transição direta das 44h para 40 horas para os setores que não concluírem a negociação coletiva até 16 de dezembro; e

a permição para que negociações coletivas possam flexibilizar o limitador mensal ou semanal para compensação das folgas.

Havia receio das confederações de que, se não concluíssem as negociações coletivas, não haveria transição e a jornada seria reduzida para 40 horas já em dezembro deste ano.

“Não existe cenário de redução de 44 para 40 horas no dia 16 de dezembro. O cenário não existe. Por quê? Porque essa foi a decisão do Congresso Nacional. Então, se o Congresso decidiu que a metodologia é 44h, 42h e 40h, assim será. Independentemente do avanço ou não das negociações”, afirmou.

Já em relação à compensação das folgas, a emenda constitucional aprovada diz que os empregadores devem assegurar, na média, dois dias de repouso semanal remunerado dentro do mês-calendário, garantido o gozo de pelo menos um dos dias dentro do período máximo de uma semana de trabalho.

Durante as discussões na audiência, confederações e centrais convergiram contra a taxatividade do texto.

“Vejo que há um acordo aqui quanto à não taxatividade. Então, nós provavelmente vamos daqui a alguns dias emitir uma decisão precisando o que foi dito por ambas as partes. Ou seja, que o limitador mensal ou semanal pode ser flexibilizado mediante a negociação coletiva. Isto é necessário, porque a emenda constitucional induz à rigidez”, afirmou.

O representante das centrais sindicais, Clemente Ganz Lúcio, rebateu as críticas das entidades e defendeu ser possível chegar a um termo no prazo estabelecido pela emenda constitucional.

“Começamos com o comércio, a primeira coisa é ‘o comércio não tem solução’. Tem. Já foi acordado, já foi assinado. Em duas semanas. Então é possível fazer”, disse.

Durante os debates, as confederações se queixaram do prazo de 60 dias para reduzir em duas horas a jornada de trabalho de 44 para 42 horas semanais e os trabalhadores disseram que quem procurou negociar conseguiu resolver dentro do prazo.

O representante da Confederação Nacional das Indústrias (CNI), Alexandre Vitorino, pediu uma transição suave e disse que preocupa à entidade a falta de mão de obra.

“Nós temos efetivamente que nesta fase discutir o que fazer sobre o dia 16 de dezembro. Mas precisamos fazer isso de uma tal forma que a transição seja suave e que ao mesmo tempo garanta que a atividade econômica não vai ter problema de suprimento de demanda de mão-de obra. Essa é a preocupação central”, afirmou.

Luciana Diniz Rodrigues, representante da Confederação Nacional do Comércio de Bens, Serviços e Turismo (CNC) disse que o período é sufocante e citou outros países, que, segundo ela, garantiram uma transição mais longa.

"Os 60 dias são sufocantes para tantas atividades que precisam ser feita tanto pelos sindicatos, quanto pelas empresas. Lá fora, a gente pode trazer como referência que o Chile deu cinco anos para chegar a 40 horas. Colômbia também cinco anos. O México, que reformou a Constituição esse ano, traz um prazo de cerca de 10 meses só pra primeira equalização”, declarou.

O ministro do Trabalho, Luiz Marinho, fez um apelo para que as confederações aceitem negociar.

O governo prepara um decreto para regulamentar a nova jornada de trabalho, com orientações aos setores da economia sobre como cumprir a emenda constitucional por meio das convenções coletivas.

“Um apelo para as confederações empresariais toparem conversar, porque isso, o relato aqui, é um retrato. Vocês sabem disso. As empresas que toparam, que procuraram chegaram a um acordo, encontraram uma solução, encontraram caminhos”, disse Marinho.

articles.title: Here are some of the House seats that Democrats didn't expect to win this year
articles.summary: Richard Hudson of North Carolina was in charge of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the organization dedicated to supporting his party's House...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina was in charge of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the organization dedicated to supporting his party's House campaigns.

But the seven-term congressman wasn't able to save his own seat this year. Republicans floundered in the state after party organizations pulled support from Michael Whatley, their U.S. Senate candidate, as he failed to gain traction against Democratic nominee Roy Cooper.

Hudson lost North Carolina's 9th district to Richard Ojeda , a former Army major who became a liberal social media phenomenon during President Donald Trump's first term. He ran multiple races in West Virginia then moved back to North Carolina, where he had served at Fort Bragg, and successfully ran against Hudson.

"Our victory is not just impressive because of how many seats we gained — although we did gain a lot — what was incredible last night was how far we reached into deep red territory," said Rep. Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Ojeda arrived on Capitol Hill this week, one of several new members who pulled off upset victories this year. Here's a look at some of them.

This district is home to NORAD, Fort Carson and the Air Force Academy, as well as the evangelical group Focus on the Family.

Although Colorado Springs has been a conservative stronghold for years, the city has been slowly turning more moderate as young families move in. Its veteran population has also been unsettled by Trump's approach to the military and the Iran war.

Jessica Killin, a Democrat and former Army captain, capitalized on this to run as a moderate against Rep. Jeff Crank, who had previously run the Colorado chapter of the conservative group Americans For Prosperity. She hammered him for falling in line behind Trump once he got into the House.

Former state lawmaker Teresa Benitez-Thompson made history as the first Democrat to win Nevada's 2nd Congressional District after her Republican opponent David Flippo's campaign was muddied by accusations of exaggerating his military record and failing to release his required financial disclosures on time.

Benitez-Thompson campaigned as a moderate with longtime northern Nevada roots, contrasting herself with Flippo, who aligned himself closely to Trump and moved from southern Nevada to join the race after longtime Republican Rep. Mark Amodei announced his retirement . Amodei refused to endorse Flippo, calling him a fraud.

For the first time ever, all of Nevada's congressional seats will be held by Democrats.

Republican Rep. Bryan Steil won all four of his previous elections in this southeast Wisconsin district by at least 9 points. Before him, former House Speaker Paul Ryan held the seat for two decades, and no Democrat had won since 1993.

All of those factors made it improbable that Democratic newcomer Mitchell Berman , running his first campaign for any office, would come out on top this year. But Berman, an emergency room nurse, tapped into voter anger and leveraged his middle-class background to beat Steil by nearly 4 points.

The outcome will ripple through Wisconsin politics because Steil was widely considered as a likely candidate for U.S. Senate down the road.

The race opened up when Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales announced he wouldn't run for reelection after admitting to an affair with a former staff member who later died by suicide. Primary voters chose Brandon Herrera , a gun enthusiast YouTuber with some 4 million subscribers and a history of caustic commentary, to run in his place.

Democrats put up Katy Padilla Stout, a lawyer and former teacher, but she was believed to have little chance. The district hadn't elected a Democrat since 2012. She ended up winning by 8 points.

This district used to be considered so blue that Republicans didn't even put up a candidate to run there in 2024. But a year later at Trump's urging, the state legislature redrew the congressional map, making it far more conservative. Democrats and their donors figured the seat was a lost cause as Democrat Leticia Gutierrez, who had previously worked in Houston city government, went up against Republican Alex Mealer, a well-financed military veteran who was active in conservative politics.

"Everyone felt it was a done deal that this was written for Republicans," said Gutierrez in an interview with The Associated Press. "They just weren't going to invest their time, money, and resources into someone that had never run a congressional campaign."

Then Gutierrez beat Mealer by a little over 15 points.

Rep. Victoria Spartz has been a wildcard in the Republican caucus, often withholding her support for legislation until the last minutes as she seeks concessions from party leadership.

But the Ukrainian-born lawmaker seemed to be a safe reelection prospect in conservative Indiana, particularly in her affluent suburban and rural district north of Indianapolis. The seat only became more red in 2021, when the state legislature removed portions of more Democratic-leaning areas of Marion County and added conservative rural tracts. Two years ago, Trump won by 17 percentage points, and Spartz won by even more.

But this year J.D. Ford, a Democratic state senator, beat Spartz by 3.4 percentage points.

There's not many red seats left in the Northeast, but one of them has been in the southeastern corner of New Jersey. The district stretches from shore resorts to the pine barrens, and it's been represented by Rep. Jeff Van Drew. He was first elected to Congress as a conservative Democrat in 2018 only to switch parties in 2020 after Trump's first impeachment.

Van Drew kept winning reelection until this week, when he lost to Zack Mullock, the Democratic mayor of Cape May. Mullock focused on Van Drew's support for the president, attacking him in a debate over the Iran war and tariffs. Van Drew argued that his connections with Trump would benefit the district.

When Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson decided to run for U.S. Senate, that left an open race for her House seat in the northeastern corner of Iowa. The Republican candidate was Joe Mitchell, a former state lawmaker, and Trump visited Dubuque just two days before the election to try to boost turnout.

Mitchell lost to Lindsay James, a Democratic state lawmaker and a minister.

"I am going to stay laser-focused on lowering costs for hard-working families here in my district because that's what they have asked me to do," James said in an interview.

Her victory was boosted by two other candidates on the ballot — one libertarian and one unaffiliated — who received more votes than James' margin over Mitchell.

Associated Press writers Hannah Fingerhut, Mike Catalini, Thomas Beaumont, Jesse Bedayn, Scott Bauer and Jessica Hill contributed to this report.

articles.title: GOP wipeout goes from bad to worse as Dems quietly score another major win with big ramifications
articles.summary: Democrats flipped legislative chambers in Wisconsin, Michigan, Arizona and other battleground states, creating trifectas that could reshape redistricting.
articles.body:
In addition to taking control of the House of Representatives, the Senate, and the majority of governorships on Tuesday, Democrats have also assumed control of the majority of state legislatures across the country for the first time in over a decade.

Heading into the election, Republicans controlled 28 of the nation's 49 bicameral state legislatures, compared with 18 controlled by Democrats, while three states had divided control. Democrats now control both chambers in 24 states, compared with 22 for Republicans. North Carolina and Texas have split legislatures, while races in Alaska and Georgia remain pending. Even if Republicans win the uncalled chambers in the pending states, Democrats will still control more state legislatures than Republicans.

Nebraska is included in the Republican count because its officially nonpartisan, unicameral legislature is led by a Republican majority.

Democrats scored major victories in several pivotal battleground states during the 2026 midterms , flipping legislative chambers and securing full control of state governments in places that will shape redistricting and election rules ahead of 2028. In Wisconsin, Democrats captured both the Assembly and Senate for the first time in years, pairing the wins with the governorship to create a trifecta.

Similar gains unfolded in Michigan , where the party flipped the House and expanded its Senate majority alongside a Democratic governor, and in Minnesota, where Democrats reclaimed the House, held the Senate, and won the governorship. Pennsylvania Democrats flipped the Senate while retaining the House, and Arizona voters handed Democrats majorities in both chambers. New Hampshire also saw Democrats flip both houses of the legislature, while the party picked up the House in Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas.

The shift gives Democrats significantly more power to shape policy across the country as state lawmakers play a central role in setting election rules, drawing congressional maps, approving budgets and advancing laws on issues ranging from abortion and guns to education and labor.

The change could also have major implications for redistricting. States will redraw congressional and legislative maps after the 2030 census, and the party controlling state government will have greater influence over how those districts are designed. Democratic control could also lead to legal battles over existing maps and efforts to alter election administration rules ahead of future presidential contests.

Democrats could similarly revive efforts to pass stricter gun laws, increase funding for public education and expand labor protections. Depending on the state, lawmakers could also target voting restrictions, expand access to mail-in and early voting, or change how elections are administered.

Results confirming Democratic control of the majority of state legislatures come days after the party captured control of both chambers of Congress and the majority of governorships.

Axios reports that 75% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic governor and 53% live in a state where Democrats control the legislature and the governorship.

"In a historic victory, Democrats now hold more than half of the seats at the state legislative level nationwide," Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee President Heather Williams said in a press release. "These victories reinforce the DLCC's national strategy to build power for Democrats all across the country. Whether competing for new majorities, breaking GOP supermajorities, or gaining seats to give Democrats more leverage to fight for their constituents, when these races have the resources they need, we can deliver wins in red, blue, and purple states alike."

Additionally, Democrats may now have the necessary votes to move forward with the National Popular Vote plan, which would bypass the Electoral College, Fox News Digital reported on Sunday .

The economy, government corruption, war in Iran and increasingly negative views of President Donald Trump's job performance created a perfect storm for Democrats, Fox News voter polling showed.

Voters cast their ballots with a bleak view of the country in their minds. Three-quarters said they felt dissatisfied or angry about how things were going, while just a quarter were satisfied or enthusiastic.

Three-quarters rated the economy negatively, a stark reversal from this point in Trump's first term, when positive ratings outnumbered negative ones by 2-to-1, as shown in the 2018 Fox News Voter Analysis survey (66% positive, 34% negative).

articles.title: Dreams, desks and selfies: Newly elected members of Congress learn their way around
articles.summary: -elect LaKesha Womack, a community organizer who stunned her own Democratic Party by defeating a well-known North Carolina Republican on her shoestring $56,0...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, a community organizer who stunned her own Democratic Party by defeating a well-known North Carolina Republican on her shoestring $56,000 campaign budget, said she's excited to arrive in Washington and show what's possible.

Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter said his win over incumbent GOP Rep. Max Miller ensures Ohio remains a very competitive swing state.

And Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot in New Jersey who said she's spent her whole life "trying to find the biggest, hardest problem to throw myself at," was ready to give Congress a try. "There's always the unknown."

They were among more than 100 newly elected members of Congress arriving in Washington this week for the start of freshmen orientation — the crush of new Democrats, many bringing a new sense of urgency after the party's sweep of the midterm elections , and the slim new class of freshmen Republicans.

"People were just looking for somebody who's going to listen to them," said Womack, who said she won by simply showing up and talking with voters.

"I'm a single mom and so I know what it's like to have to live on a budget and figure out how am I going to feed my family," she said. "And that's what people want to fight for them in Washington right now."

New-member orientation creates an unusual mash-up on Capitol Hill, as the newcomers are arriving and the exiting lawmakers begin to clear out, all in preparation for the peaceful transfer of power on Jan. 3, when lawmakers are sworn in and the new Congress begins.

This week's orientation includes training sessions and ritzy receptions for the newcomers, and for the defeated or those retiring it's the start of figuring out what's next. Briefing rooms are filled with information about office setup, payroll and benefits, and there's a room to take official portraits.

It's also the time for the House and Senate to hold internal party elections for their new leaders, ahead of a public vote in January for the speaker of the House.

"I'm looking forward to learning as much as I can and being the best representative I can be for my district," said Poindexter as he arrived at the nearby Navy Yard hotel where lawmakers converged.

The Capitol was a changed place as the members-elect started meeting up with their colleagues and getting to know their way around the place.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan was swarmed by young people in the Capitol basement, taking pictures with the progressive star who is also the first Muslim in the Senate.

Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico paid a visit to the outgoing Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his own primary for reelection. President Donald Trump backed Cornyn's rival, Ken Paxton, who was defeated.

"I'm so grateful for his advice and his guidance as I try to fill his big shoes," Talarico said of Cornyn as he walked through the Senate between orientation events. He said he wants to meet with Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas as well.

And Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton of Illinois snapped a photo with new Democratic senators-elect including Talarico, El-Sayed, Annie Andrews , Roy Cooper , Peggy Flanagan , Josh Turek and others.

"First Freshmen Senator selfie! Couldn't ask for a better team," she posted as the caption.

Among them was former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown , who defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted, a Trump-backed favorite, for a comeback. Brown was in the Senate for 18 years before he lost two years ago to GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno, but he still joined his freshmen colleagues for their orientation.

"I've actually learned some things," said Brown, who was celebrating his 74th birthday on Monday. "I've gotten to know my colleagues."

Leadership elections test the new members

One of the first decisions the incoming lawmakers will make happens even before they're sworn into office, as they huddle with their parties in private meetings to choose House and Senate leadership.

Congressional offices are being bombarded with phone calls and social media messages pushing Democrats to dump their current choices — House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer — in favor of a fresh start.

Jeffries scoffed when questioned Monday if he had support— the typically low-key leader flashing confidence he would have the votes. He is on track to make history as the nation's first Black American to become speaker of the House.

Progressive lawmakers, in particular, are agitating for change reflective of voters' sweeping turnout for Democrats, especially in the Senate . Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan announced they would not support Schumer.

Sen.-elect Chris Pappas, D-N.H. — who was darting back and forth between his day job as an outgoing member of the House and his new one as an incoming senator — said their class is "a new generation of leadership that wants to do things differently and shake up Washington."

He said he wants to meet with Schumer and will later decide who he will support, if anyone challenges him.

Republicans chose their new leaders after House Speaker Mike Johnson decided to step aside following the party's election defeat. Ohio Rep. Jim Jordon won the race against the No. 2 Republican Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana to become the minority leader, continuing a rivalry stretching to 2023, before Johnson rose to power.

Senate Republicans tapped Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to stay on as leader, despite those agitating for a change.

As the week began, the House Chaplain Margaret Kibben opened Monday's session with a prayer, "some of us enjoying victories and others enduring disheartening defeats."

On the Democratic side, the new Congress will see many milestones — Flanagan will be the first Native American female U.S. senator, Pappas the first gay male senator, and more.

Rep. Suzan DelBene, the House Democrats' campaign chief, called the party's candidates "all very unique."

"We had firefighters, ministers, mayors, veterans, teachers, farmers, prosecutors, union leaders, law enforcement, doctors, journalists and even a Grammy award-winning musician," she said earlier.

"They understand that their job title is representative, not rubber stamp."

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, hosted a reception in the Capitol's stately Statuary Hall for the House Republicans, whose shrinking numbers left the party lopsided, their minority made up of mostly white men.

articles.title: A note to ‘46’: Donald Trump’s private message to Joe Biden emerges in new White House memoir
articles.summary: President Donald Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result having been stolen from him by Democratic forces...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result having been stolen from him by Democratic forces, privately lauded incoming President Joe Biden as someone he believed "will be true to yourself and the American people."

That sentiment, along with others, was part of the letter Trump left for Biden upon leaving office in January 2021. Biden showed the note to some members of his staff after his inauguration in 2021 but didn't let anyone read it, describing it later that day as "very generous" but otherwise saying he considered it to be private.

Inclusion of the letter in Biden's "Promise Me, America," his White House memoir slated for release Nov. 17, was first reported Tuesday by The New York Times. The Associated Press has reviewed a photocopy of the two-page letter, handwritten in Trump's trademark black Sharpie on White House stationery and addressed "To '46,'" denoting Biden's place as the 46th U.S. president.

"Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats," Trump wrote. "Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people."

At the time of transition, Biden was said to have been surprised by how gracious he thought the letter was, given the animosity between the political rivals. Trump had opted out of other presidential traditions, like attending Biden's inauguration , or hosting the incoming president and first lady for tea at the White House.

Trump has said he thought it was up to Biden to share the letter, calling it "a nice note" during a September 2023 interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," adding, "I took a lot of time in thinking about it."

Elsewhere in the memoir, the first excerpt of which was published Monday by the Atlantic, Biden wrote of the deep damage Trump has inflicted, with an administration determined to "tear down institutions and inflame hatreds."

Lamenting Trump's Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, Biden wrote of Trump's "dismissive and destructive nature," describing his predecessor and successor as someone "who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else's accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down."

But Biden's harshest characterization so far was focused on Trump's role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, as Congress met to certify the 2020 election, which Biden had won. Writing that Trump "led an insurrection," Biden said Trump's "goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office."

"What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten," Biden wrote. "It should follow him to his grave."

Asked for comment on both the letter and Biden's memoir, White House communications director Steven Cheung called the former president "a disgrace" who "should have heeded the President's wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies."

articles.title: Thune elected Senate GOP leader after bruising showdown with critics
articles.summary: Sen. John Thune (S.D.) won reelection to serve another term as Senate Republican leader Tuesday after a bruising showdown with conservative critics in the Senate Republican conference. A Senate GOP aide announced late in the afternoon that Thune had been reelected as leader “by acclamation,” despite objections raised by a handful of GOP senators over…
articles.body:
Sen. John Thune (S.D.) won reelection to serve another term as Senate Republican leader Tuesday after a bruising showdown with conservative critics in the Senate Republican conference.

A Senate GOP aide announced late in the afternoon that Thune had been reelected as leader “by acclamation,” despite objections raised by a handful of GOP senators over proceeding with the vote this week.

A Republican conference meeting that was initially expected to last a few hours turned into an all-day affair after Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) threatened to walk out of the meeting if a vote on the new leadership team was held immediately.

Johnson, who has clashed with Thune over advancing a third budget reconciliation bill to fund the Defense Department, demanded a delay of the leadership election. He picked up the support of more than a dozen colleagues angry over the huge Republican losses in last week’s election.

Fifteen Republican senators voted to delay Thune’s reelection — roughly a third of the next Senate GOP conference.

Johnson walked out of the meeting right after Republican colleagues voted to proceed, following through on his boycott threat. He and several other GOP senators, including Senate Steering Committee Chair Rick Scott (Fla.) and Sen. Mike Lee (Utah), demanded that Thune lay out a plan for how he would manage the lame-duck session.

They pressed Thune to commit to bring a budget reconciliation package to the Senate floor during the lame-duck session and use it as a vehicle to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a package of election security rules requiring people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote and present photo ID when casting a ballot.

The conservatives lobbied Thune to cancel the weeklong Thanksgiving recess to allow for more time to pass a budget resolution and follow-up reconciliation bill to fund the Defense Department over Democratic objections.

Thune gave some ground by floating the possibility of keeping the Senate in session the rest of the week to work on President Trump’s agenda. Senators were scheduled to be on recess until next Monday in observance of Veterans Day.

“We’ll see,” Thune said when asked about working through Veterans Day.

He defended his record over the past two years, arguing that Senate Republicans passed one of “the most consequential” bills of his career when it approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last summer.

“As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is what would you have me do differently?” the Senate leader asked.

“I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected and got a lot of stuff done. Last summer, that bill — in my view, in my time in Congress — is the most consequential piece of legislation I’ve worked on that had a lot of new ideas,” he said, citing new tax policy and fiscal reform.

Thune agreed to a conference-wide statement pledging to make every effort to advance a budget resolution and budget reconciliation package to fund the Defense Department in the lame-duck session, according to GOP sources familiar with the meeting.

GOP senators also pledged to make every effort to confirm Trump’s judicial and executive branch nominees before Jan. 1.

Thune said that Republicans fared poorly in last week’s election because of political headwinds created by factors “out of our control.”

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices, and I think that’s what the election was about,” he said. “I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else more I could have done. The amount of money we raised was record.”

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) joined the calls to postpone Thune’s reelection as leader.

He criticized Republican leaders in Congress for failing to advance legislation to address high gas prices and high healthcare costs before the midterm election.

“If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats, minimum, that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” Hawley said. “It’s easy to blame other people but we need to look at what happened here.

“What did we to get the price of gas down? Nothing. What did we do to get the price of healthcare down? Nothing,” he said.

Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), a moderate who represents an important swing state, also favored delaying the election.

But they were outvoted by GOP colleagues who wanted to end the intraparty squabbling as soon as possible and move forward on the lame-duck agenda without having to worry about the distraction of a leadership fight.

After hours of contentious discussion, no Republican senator stood up to challenge Thune, who was elected majority leader two years ago.

Many GOP senators blame last week’s midterms wipeout on Trump’s unpopularity.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), Thune’s one-time rival to become Republican leader, blamed Trump’s unpopularity and voter anger over “corruption” for Democrat James Talarico’s victory over Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race.

“Corruption was an issue not only at the local level or the state level but also at the national level, too. And I think that contributed to the landslide that swept almost everybody in the process,” the outgoing Texas senator told reporters Monday.

Thune acknowledged after the meeting that voters’ concerns about corruption in Washington was a factor in Republican losses and pledged to push legislation to ban stock trading by members of Congress next year.

“Clearly the Democrats tried to make that issue in a lot of states,” he said. “It had some resonance out there, which is, again, why I think it’s important that as we move forward, we’re looking for ways to differentiate and distinguish what we’re for,” referring to bills to ban stock trading by lawmakers.

images.caption: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) arrives for a press conference after the weekly policy luncheon on Sept. 29, 2026.

articles.title: White House announces funds for law enforcement programme in several cities
articles.summary: Trump administration awarded more than $60m each to St Louis, Missouri, and Jackson, Mississippi, in crime push.
articles.body:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has said that it will award the cities of St Louis, Missouri, and Jackson, Mississippi, more than $60m each to expand law enforcement resources as part of a bid to combat violent crime.

The White House stated in a social media post on Tuesday that the so-called “Model Cities Initiative” would help the municipalities increase their capacity for prosecutions and policing activities.

“The Model Cities Initiative reflects the Trump Administration’s commitment to reducing crime across the country and ensuring the safety of every American,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release describing the programme last month.

The initiative has said that it will distribute nearly $300m for such efforts among the cities of St Louis and Jackson, along with Jacksonville, Florida, and Baton Rouge, Louisiana.

The Trump administration has promoted a largely punitive approach to combatting crime in cities across the country, including controversial steps such as the deployment of the National Guard to large, Democrat-led cities that have drawn accusations of executive overreach, civil liberties violations and political intimidation.

While Trump and his supporters have credited their policies with a drop in violent crime, that trend predates his return to office and has taken place in cities with a wide variety of approaches towards criminal justice across the country.

Homicides in St Louis, for example, have been falling for several years after a brief surge during the COVID-19 pandemic, and hit their lowest levels in more than a decade during the first half of 2026.

While Democratic officials have denounced Trump’s crackdowns, some Republican-led states have embraced them.

The government deployed members of several federal agencies to the city of Memphis , Tennessee, governed by Democrats at the local level but located in a Republican-led state.

The Trump administration has touted that effort as an inspiration for the Model Cities Initiative along with other cases, such as Washington, DC.

The government has hailed the Memphis deployment as a success, but some residents and civil liberties groups have accused the task force of widespread civil rights violations and excessive force.

A video released earlier this month as part of an investigation into a shooting by a member of the Tennessee National Guard, deployed in Memphis as part of Trump’s task force, showed the soldiers aiming their guns at a man as he lay dying on the street after being shot in the back.

articles.title: Justice Department sues Lyft for alleged discrimination against disabled passengers
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) is suing ride-hailing company Lyft for discrimination against disabled passengers, alleging that Lyft has denied service and imposed fees against disabled passengers. The lawsuit, filed in the Northern District of California, alleges that Lyft drivers have denied service to passengers with disabilities and then charged those riders cancellation fees. It…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) is suing ride-hailing company Lyft for discrimination against disabled passengers, alleging that Lyft has denied service and imposed fees against disabled passengers.

The lawsuit , filed in the Northern District of California, alleges that Lyft drivers have denied service to passengers with disabilities and then charged those riders cancellation fees. It specifically identifies circumstances of denials for passengers with service animals and stowable wheelchairs.

In the lawsuit, the DOJ said it receives thousands of complaints each year and accuses the company of violating the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

“Lyft has discriminated against individuals with disabilities, in violation of Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act … through its policies and practices of denying or providing unequal services to individuals with disabilities, including individuals with service animals or individuals who use stowable wheelchairs or mobility devices,” the lawsuit reads.

In a statement to The Hill, a Lyft spokesperson said the company disagrees with the allegations and that its policies already protect riders with disabilities.

“We have long-standing policies that require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices for years, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including losing access to Lyft permanently,” the spokesperson said. “We’ve worked with the DOJ throughout its review, and we’ll keep working to make sure every rider can get where they need to go.”

The DOJ has sued Lyft before, and the company settled a lawsuit over similar claims about discrimination against people with disabilities in 2020. The department also sued Lyft’s competitor Uber for similar claims on two separate occasions, in 2022 and 2025.

The department said it is seeking a court order to prevent Lyft from discrimination, as well as to force it to modify its policies and better train its drivers. The DOJ is also seeking a payout to the affected individuals, several of whom are named in the lawsuit.

In a statement, U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakin said the DOJ will “devote all the resources necessary” to the case.

“We take these allegations of misconduct seriously and, like our case against Uber for similar discriminatory conduct, we will devote all the resources necessary to make things right. The stakes are high and we owe those with disabilities nothing less,” Missakian said.

articles.title: Florida AG subpoenas DSA over potential illegal funding from Cuba and China
articles.summary: James Uthmeier says a subpoena targets the Democratic Socialists of America over possible foreign donations tied to Cuba and China delegations.
articles.body: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that his office issued an investigative subpoena to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) to investigate whether the organization accepted contributions from "foreign sources of concern," including entities in Cuba and China. "Our laws prohibit accepting contributions from foreign sources of concern," Uthmeier said in a video statement. "We will not allow foreign adversaries to influence Florida through the backdoor of non-private fundraising." The subpoena demands documents related to recent DSA delegations to China and Cuba, where organization members met with Cuban government officials, to determine if the DSA violated Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, according to Uthmeier. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA ACTIVISTS SIGNED PLEDGE TO SUPPORT, DEFEND 'CHINESE SOCIALISM' Uthmeier did not detail specific criminal allegations or name individuals accused of violating state law. The DSA has repeatedly praised the Cuban regime and routinely advocates for lifting American sanctions and ending the U.S. embargo against Havana. RNC WARNS DEMOCRATS FACE 'POLITICAL SUICIDE' AFTER DSA PRAISES FIDEL CASTRO, DEMANDS RUBIO'S PROSECUTION The organization has sent multiple delegations to Cuba in recent years. During a 2023 trip, DSA members met privately with Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel and sought to establish formal communication channels with government ministries, according to a State Department report released in July. The legal action comes shortly after several DSA-backed candidates won races across federal, state, and local levels in last week's elections. articles.title: Democrats now control majority of state legislatures. Here’s the 6 they flipped
articles.summary: Democrats are poised to take control of a majority of state legislatures for the first time in 16 years after the party secured sweeping wins in the midterm elections. Twenty-four state legislatures will be under full Democratic control starting in January, with the party flipping 12 total individual chambers. Republicans will control both chambers in…
articles.body:
Democrats are poised to take control of a majority of state legislatures for the first time in 16 years after the party secured sweeping wins in the midterm elections.

Twenty-four state legislatures will be under full Democratic control starting in January, with the party flipping 12 total individual chambers. Republicans will control both chambers in 22 states, down from 28 states prior to the election.

Two states — North Carolina and Texas — will both have divided legislatures, after Democrats flipped control of the lower chambers only.

Control of the Alaska and Georgia legislatures hangs in the balance pending final election results. The Peach State appears to be headed toward a split legislature, while Alaska is controlled by a bipartisan coalition.

Democrats are also expected to gain trifectas in 22 states. If this is attained, 53 percent of Americans could live in state with both a Democrat-controlled governor’s mansion and legislature, according to Axios .

Here are the six states expected to switch to fully Democrat-controlled legislatures in 2027:

Both chambers in Arizona’s legislature are expected to switch from Republican to Democratic control, breaking the hold the GOP’s had on the state capitol for more than 60 years.

Democrats will now have a 37-23 seat majority in the state’s lower chamber and a 20-10 advantage in the upper chamber, according to the Arizona Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee (ADLCC).

Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs (D), who won her reelection race last week, celebrated her party’s trifecta in a social media post Tuesday.

“When I co-founded the ADLCC in 2014, there were so few Democrats in the state Senate that we joked we could all share one pizza,” she wrote. “Now, Arizona will have a Democratic trifecta for the first time in 60 years. We’re going to need a lot more pizza.”

Michigan’s House flipped blue and Democrats maintained their majority in the state Senate chamber on Election Day, establishing full Democratic control.

With Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson (D) at the helm, Democrats in the Wolverine State have secured a trifecta they lost when Republicans took the House majority in 2024.

“Once again, we’ve secured a Democratic trifecta here in Michigan that is ready to lower costs and get stuff done on day one,” outgoing Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) wrote in a social media post on Nov. 4.

Minnesota Democrats broke a tie in the state House in the midterms and kept their control of the state Senate chamber this election cycle.

The lower chamber has held its 67-67 balance since the 2024 election, with special elections giving each party brief advantages since. Republican state Rep. Lisa Demuth has served as the Minnesota House Speaker since 2025.

Minnesota state Rep. Zack Stephenson (D) will serve as the chamber’s next leader. Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), who won Minnesota’s gubernatorial race last week, congratulated Stephenson on his appointment in a social media post .

“I can’t wait to work with you! Lots of challenges and good work ahead,” Klobuchar wrote.

Democrats in New Hampshire are expected to flip control of both chambers of the state legislature, while Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte held the Granite State’s governor’s mansion.

Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, characterized the party’s victories in the state House and Senate as equivalent to a “political earthquake” in a press release after Election Day.

“By flipping not just one, but both chambers, Democrats won full control of the legislature for the first time since 2018,” Williams said. “On a historic night for Democrats across the country, this victory has fundamentally shifted the balance of power in New Hampshire.”

Keystone State Democrats flipped the Senate from Republican control and maintained their majority in the lower legislative chamber on Election Day.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) celebrated the beginning of a “new chapter” with a Democratic trifecta in the commonwealth in a statement shared to social media Thursday.

The state’s Senate Minority Leader Jay Costa (D) expressed his party’s eagerness to take over the upper legislative chamber following the Democratic win.

“Senate Democrats are ready to get to work in the majority, moving bills that have languished in committee for far too long,” he wrote on social media last week. “The obstructionists are out, and a trifecta is in. Let’s go.”

Both of Wisconsin’s legislative chambers will switch from GOP to Democratic control in the coming weeks.

Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley won the race to replace outgoing Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers (D), ensuring single-party control in the state for the first time since 2010.

Devin Remiker, chair of Wisconsin’s Democratic Party, said the party’s new trifecta was “more than a decade in the making” in a statement following the midterm election.
